title: Fratelli Tutti (2020)
hook: Francis retells the good Samaritan for a divided world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the throwaway culture. Your line was nothing and no one thrown away. Did the thing get fixed, and did the message get sent? Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

Two words, Italian: fratelli tutti. All brothers. Francis of Assisi used them to address his brothers and sisters, the way someone might open a letter with dear friends. Pope Francis took them for the title of a letter about a world split into camps: nations against nations, neighbors who won't speak, strangers left on the side of the road. And to make his case, he didn't open with a theory. He sat down with a story Jesus told, about a man beaten and left half dead on the road to Jericho, and asked the reader a question. Which one of these people are you? Today is that letter.
screen: `FRATELLI TUTTI: ALL BROTHERS.` → `A WORLD SPLIT INTO CAMPS.` → `WHICH ONE ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: First, the road. In Luke's Gospel, robbers strip a traveler and leave him by the road. A priest comes by and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, someone the listeners would have expected to keep his distance, stops, binds the wounds, and pays for the man's care at an inn. Second, the mirror. Francis says each of us can find ourselves in every character. Sometimes the wounded man. Sometimes the robbers, or the ones who pass by. He asks how often we look away, busy, sure it's someone else's job, and he notices that the passersby were religious men. Faith alone, in this story, doesn't make anyone stop. Third, the question flipped. A lawyer had asked Jesus, who is my neighbor? Jesus answers with the story, then turns the question around, in the Douay-Rheims: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?" Francis leans on that turn. The question isn't who counts as my neighbor. It's whether I'll become one. Fourth, the title. Jesus tells his disciples, "all you are brethren." Francis widens that circle to every person, across borders and parties and faiths. In the letter he writes of his conversations with a Muslim leader, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, and of their shared call to fraternity. And the story ends with an instruction anyone can carry: "Go, and do thou in like manner." This week we walked from the gospel of life, through the death penalty, Caritas in Veritate, Laudato Si', two cries, and the throwaway culture, to this road. The same thread ran through all of it: no one is a stranger to be passed by.
screen: `A MAN LEFT ON THE ROAD TO JERICHO.` · `WE ARE EVERY CHARACTER.` · `NOT WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR, BUT BECOME ONE.` · `ALL YOU ARE BRETHREN.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse stopping. Settle, and breathe. Picture a place you pass every day: a corner, a hallway, a parking lot, a group chat. Who is usually there, on the edge, that you walk past? Maybe not from unkindness. Maybe just from hurry. Hold that person in mind. Imagine slowing down instead. What would stopping look like, really? A greeting, a question, five minutes. If you pray, you can ask God for the Samaritan's eyes. If you don't, simply hold the picture of yourself stopping. The bell holds the time.
Fratelli Tutti. All brothers: Francis's letter on fraternity, built around the good Samaritan. Today's word, and the end of this week.
Your line: all brothers and sisters. Today, stop for one person you'd normally pass, and give them a few unhurried minutes. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes and schools study Fratelli Tutti, often alongside the parable of the good Samaritan, and some use it in interfaith gatherings and in ministries that visit people on the margins.

fork.setup: a man lies beaten on the road to Jericho. a priest and a Levite have passed by. what does the Samaritan do?
options: pass by on the other side.
stop, bind his wounds, and pay for his care.
call out that help will come later.
fork.reveal: the Samaritan stops, binds the wounds and pays at the inn. Jesus ends: "Go, and do thou in like manner."

original.note: Italian, not Latin: all brothers, the words Francis of Assisi used to address his brothers and sisters.

trapdoor: what you thought: a letter only for men, or only for Catholics.
what it means: a letter calling every person a brother or sister, built around the good Samaritan's choice to stop.
what a scholar hears: a title taken from Francis of Assisi's Admonitions, and Jesus's question turned from who is my neighbor to who became one.
